interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the two counters at a mesh ticking up together, tooth for tooth, so the two gears turn opposite ways, when you turn the driver by its rim.
interactive.title: The gear board
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on a gear board. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. The board is a grid of pegs. One peg holds the driver, the gear you turn, with a ring round its rim to drag. Gears wait in a tray, and you drag them onto pegs. A gear meshes with any gear it touches. Each gear shows its tooth count at its centre, one marked tooth on its rim, a revolution counter, and an arrow for the way it turns. At every mesh sit two counters, one for each gear, that tick up as teeth pass. Drag the driver round by its rim and everything it meshes with turns. Each tooth on one gear pushes one tooth on the other past the mesh, so the two counters at a mesh always match. At the mesh the teeth of both gears move the same way, so the two gears turn opposite ways. Each mesh flips the direction, so along a line the arrows alternate. Drop a gear that closes a loop. With an even number of gears the loop turns. With an odd number, the last gear and the first both try to turn the same way, so the driver will not move, and the mesh you closed last is drawn in red. The counters give the speed rule too. A gear passes its own tooth count each time it turns once, so the teeth it passes in a minute are its speed × its teeth. The two counters at a mesh match, so n₁T₁ = n₂T₂, where n is a gear's speed in rev/min and T its number of teeth. The screens, in order. Screen 1, show, Teeth pass one for one: a 12-tooth driver meshes with a 20-tooth gear. Words: "Where two gears mesh, each tooth pushes one tooth on the other gear. So at the mesh, the teeth of both gears move the same way. That turns the two gears opposite ways." Then "Turn the driver by its rim." Read: the 12-tooth driver turns clockwise and the 20-tooth gear turns anticlockwise, and the two counters at the mesh always show the same count. Screen 2, do, Five in a line: five gears in a line, still. "The first gear turns clockwise. Which way does the fifth turn?" Choices: Clockwise (right), Anticlockwise. Hint: "Each mesh flips the direction. Count the meshes." Why: five gears make four meshes, so four flips: anticlockwise, clockwise, anticlockwise, clockwise, and the fifth turns the driver's way. After Check the line turns. Screen 3, show, Odd and even: lines of two, three, four and five gears turn side by side. Words: "Each mesh flips the direction, so the arrows alternate along a line. An odd number of gears turns the last one the driver's way. An even number turns it the other way." Read: the same three sentences. Screen 4, do, Mixed sizes: four gears in a line with 12, 40, 16 and 30 teeth, the driver clockwise. "Which way does the fourth gear turn?" Choices: Clockwise, Anticlockwise (right). Hint on Clockwise: "Size changes the speed, not the direction. Count the meshes." Why: three meshes make three flips, so the fourth turns anticlockwise; the big 40-tooth gear turns slower, but it still flips the direction once. Screen 5, show, Close the loop: a triangle of three gears, each meshing with the other two, locked, with its last mesh in red; beside it a ring of four gears turning. Words: "Close three gears into a triangle, and the third meets the first. Both try to turn the same way, so their teeth at that mesh would have to move opposite ways. Neither can give way, so the triangle locks." Read: the triangle of three is locked, its last mesh drawn in red, and the ring of four turns. Screen 6, do, Which loop turns: three loops lying flat on the board, of five, six and seven gears. "Which loop turns?" Choices, in a row that wraps at phone width: The loop of five, The loop of six (right), The loop of seven. Hint: "Round a loop the directions alternate. The last gear must end up opposite the first." Why: six is even, so the sixth gear turns opposite to the first, as their mesh needs; five and seven are odd, so they lock, whatever the gears' sizes. Screen 7, show, Count the teeth: a 12-tooth driver meshes with a 36-tooth gear, with the mesh counters and each gear's revolution counter. Words: "Each tooth that passes on one gear pushes one past on the other. Three turns of the 12-tooth driver pass 36 teeth, which is one turn of the 36-tooth gear. So speed × teeth is the same on both gears: n₁T₁ = n₂T₂." Read: three turns of the 12-tooth driver pass 36 teeth and turn the 36-tooth gear once. Screen 8, do, typed, How fast: "A 12-tooth gear turns at 60 rev/min and drives a 36-tooth gear. How fast does the 36-tooth gear turn?" A typed answer: 20 rev/min, a whole number. Slips: 180 rev/min, "That makes the bigger gear faster. It has more teeth to take in, so it turns slower."; 3 rev/min, "That is the ratio, 36 ÷ 12. Divide the speed by it." Hint: "Work out the teeth a minute through the mesh first." Why: 60 × 12 = 720 teeth a minute pass the mesh, and 720 ÷ 36 = 20 rev/min. The 36-tooth gear's revolution counter shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 9, show, The idler: a 20-tooth gear set between the 12-tooth driver and the 36-tooth gear. Words: "Put a 20-tooth gear between the two. It passes on the same 720 teeth a minute, so the last gear still turns at 20 rev/min. Now it turns the driver's way, and the middle gear is called an idler gear." Read: with a 20-tooth idler between them, the idler turns at 36 rev/min and the 36-tooth gear still turns at 20 rev/min, now the driver's way. Screen 10, do, typed, Through an idler: "A 15-tooth gear at 1200 rev/min drives a 40-tooth idler. The idler drives a 45-tooth gear. How fast does the 45-tooth gear turn?" A typed answer: 400 rev/min, a whole number. Slips: 450 rev/min, "That is the idler's speed. It passes the same teeth a minute on to the last gear."; 3600 rev/min, "That makes the bigger gear faster. Turn the ratio the other way up." Hint: "The idler passes on the driver's teeth a minute." Why: 1200 × 15 = 18,000 teeth a minute pass both meshes, and 18,000 ÷ 45 = 400 rev/min; the idler only flips the direction. Screen 11, do, typed, The winch: "A winch motor turns an 18-tooth gear at 1440 rev/min. It drives a 72-tooth gear on the drum. How fast does the drum turn?" A typed answer: 360 rev/min, a whole number. Slips: 5760 rev/min, "That makes the drum faster than the motor. The 72-tooth gear has more teeth to take in."; 4 rev/min, "That is the ratio, 72 ÷ 18. Divide the speed by it." Hint: "Teeth a minute first, then divide by the drum gear's teeth." Why: 1440 × 18 = 25,920 teeth a minute, and 25,920 ÷ 72 = 360 rev/min. Screen 12, do, typed, How many teeth: "A 24-tooth gear turns at 300 rev/min. The gear it drives must turn at 100 rev/min. How many teeth does that gear need?" A typed answer: 72 teeth, a whole number. Slip: 8 teeth, "That gear would turn faster than the driver. A slower gear needs more teeth." Hint: "The teeth a minute are the same on both gears." Why: 300 × 24 = 7200 teeth a minute, and 7200 ÷ 100 = 72 teeth. Screen 13, do, Add a fifth: a ring of four gears turning. "You fit a fifth gear into the ring. What happens when you turn the driver?" Choices, in a row that wraps at phone width: It still turns; It locks (right); It turns, but slower. Hint on It still turns: "Count the gears in the ring now." Hint on It turns, but slower: "Sizes change the speed in a line. An odd loop cannot turn at all." Why: five is odd, so round the ring the fifth gear and the first both try to turn the same way, and nothing moves, whatever the sizes. After Check the fifth gear drops in and the new mesh goes red.
interactive.ignores: The gears are drawn rigid, with teeth that fit perfectly and never slip. Real gears have a little play between their teeth, so a locked loop may rock slightly, but it still cannot turn. The board turns as fast as you drag, so a speed in rev/min comes from a puzzle's numbers, not from your finger. The red mesh is just the one closed last: the lock belongs to the whole loop. Every gear lies flat in one plane with its teeth on the outside. A ring gear has its teeth on the inside, and it turns the same way as a gear meshing inside it. Bevel gears, meeting at an angle, follow other direction rules too. Speed × teeth is the same on both sides of every kind of mesh.

explain.text:
Where two gears mesh, their teeth pass one for one. So neighbouring gears turn opposite ways, and both pass the same number of teeth a minute. Look at the point where two gears meet, their [[mesh]]. Each tooth on the driver pushes a tooth on the other gear along with it. So at the mesh the teeth of both gears move the same way, and the two gears turn opposite ways.[^1] Say the driver turns clockwise, with the next gear on its right. The driver's right-hand teeth move down. They push the next gear's left-hand teeth down too, and that turns it anticlockwise.

So each mesh flips the direction. Along a line of gears with their teeth on the outside, the directions alternate. An odd number of gears in a line turns the last one the driver's way. An even number turns it the other way. A gear's size changes how fast it turns, not which way. One gear set between two others makes them turn the same way. It is called an [[idler gear]]. Now close a line into a loop, so the last gear meshes with the first. With an even number of gears, the last turns opposite to the first, as their mesh needs, and the loop turns. With an odd number, the last gear and the first try to turn the same way. At their mesh the teeth would have to move in opposite directions, and neither can give way. An odd number of gears in a closed loop in one plane will not turn, whatever their sizes and tooth counts.[^3]

The same count gives the speed. In any minute, both gears pass the same number of teeth through the mesh. A gear passes its whole tooth count each time it turns once. So the teeth it passes in a minute are its speed in rev/min × its number of teeth. Call the speed n and the number of teeth T. Then n₁T₁ = n₂T₂ for any two meshed gears.[^2] A 12-tooth driver at 60 rev/min passes 60 × 12 = 720 teeth a minute. A 36-tooth gear takes in those 720 teeth, so it turns at 720 ÷ 36 = 20 rev/min. Turn the ratio upside down and you get 60 × 36 ÷ 12 = 180 rev/min. That cannot be right, because the bigger gear has three times as many teeth to take in. An idler passes on the same 720 teeth a minute, whatever its size. So it changes the output's direction, not its speed.

In a winch, a small gear on the fast motor drives a gear with many more teeth on the drum. So the drum turns far slower than the motor. Textbooks add that the slower gear turns harder, which is where the winch's extra pull comes from. **Meshed gears pass teeth one for one, so neighbours turn opposite ways.[^1] Speed × teeth is the same on both: n₁T₁ = n₂T₂.[^2]**

analogy.text: A loaded transformer balances its ampere-turns: I₁N₁ = I₂N₂, so the winding with more turns carries less current. A gear pair balances speed × teeth the same way, n₁T₁ = n₂T₂, so the gear with more teeth turns slower.
analogy.breaks: The transformer's balance is only nearly true, because the primary also carries a small magnetising current. The gear count is exact, since every tooth that passes the mesh is counted on both gears. The ampere-turn balance also says nothing about direction, while each mesh between outside teeth reverses it.

practice.text:
- Before you turn a machine's gears by hand, isolate it and lock it off. Keep fingers clear of any mesh that can move.
- Number the gears from the driver, and note which gear meshes with which.
- Direction: flip it at every mesh between outside teeth. In a line, an odd number of gears turns the last one the driver's way, and an even number the other way.
- Loops: count the gears in any closed loop. An odd number lying flat in one plane locks.
- Speed: work out the teeth a minute through the first mesh, the driver's speed × its teeth. Divide that by each gear's teeth to get its speed.

**Rule of thumb:** the gear with more teeth turns slower than its partner. An idler flips the direction and leaves the output speed alone.

**Worked example:** a 20-tooth gear on a motor at 1450 rev/min drives a 25-tooth idler, which drives a 100-tooth gear. Teeth a minute: 1450 × 20 = 29,000. The idler turns at 29,000 ÷ 25 = 1160 rev/min. The output turns at 29,000 ÷ 100 = 290 rev/min. Three gears in a line, so it turns the motor's way.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking meshed gears turn the same way. Their teeth move together at the mesh, so the gears turn opposite ways.
- Turning the ratio upside down, so the bigger gear comes out faster.
- Letting the idler's teeth change the output speed. It passes on the same teeth a minute.
- Letting a gear's size decide its direction. Count the meshes instead.
- Missing an odd loop. Three gears that all mesh with each other cannot turn.
